notes:
I've organised these notes by verse. A few gaps first. I couldn't find any Catholic or Orthodox material (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), nothing from bibleodyssey.org, and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter, so those are left out. The Pulpit Commentary text I read stops partway through v. 11. That means vv. 12–14 (who Nathan, Levi and Shimei were) are thinly covered. Where a page labels a commentator's tradition I say so; otherwise I don't add one.

**v. 1**
- God is called Creator at the start so readers know he is in control and can do what he predicts. The section begins with praise for God's creative power (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-12/
- The Pulpit Commentary says God's attributes are mentioned here that all may believe that what he has promised, that he is able to perform. It reads "forms the spirit of man" as God creating, shaping and guiding human souls. It also says "Israel" here means the Messianic people of God, a "new" Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm
- Precept Austin argues the verse refutes Deism, the idea that God made the world and then stepped back: God is actively, continually involved with His Creation. It insists "Israel" means the literal nation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah-12-commentary

**v. 2**
- The Pulpit Commentary: hostile nations crowd round Jerusalem like thirsty men round a bowl of wine, and the drink proves deadly. The "cup" image often stands for God's judgment (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). It says the line about Judah is hard to translate. Its preferred sense is that the whole country, not just the city, will be invaded. It rules out readings where Judah joins the attack on Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm
- The ESV Global Study Bible (quoted on Precept Austin): The Lord will force the nations to drink of his judgment and in doing so they will become so intoxicated by his wrath that they will stumble. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah_commentaries

**v. 3**
- The Pulpit Commentary: Jerusalem is a stone too heavy to lift, and it cuts those who try. It mentions Jerome's idea of an allusion to local strength-testing stones, but doubts that custom existed in Zechariah's day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm
- Guzik calls Jerusalem a problem no one can solve. He quotes Dave Hunt, who says all nations being involved in Israel's fate has occurred exactly as prophesied and is still in the process of being implemented. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-12/

**v. 4**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the horses stand for the enemy's army. Astonishment, madness, and blindness are threatened against Israel in Deuteronomy 28:28; here they arc inflicted on the enemy. The panicked riders turn on each other (Haggai 2:22). "Keep a watchful eye" means God looks on Judah with favour and protects it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm
- Guzik: this will find its ultimate fulfillment in the last battle at the end of the age, but we may also find earlier fulfillments. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-12/

**v. 5**
- The Pulpit Commentary: seeing the enemy beaten, Judah's leaders drop their old jealousy of Jerusalem. They trust that God chose the city, and they see her success as a sign of his protection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm

**v. 6**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the leaders are like a pan of fire set among dry sticks, so the victory is easy and complete. Jerusalem stays firm "in her own place." It applies this to the church, against which hell's gates will not prevail. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm
- Guzik: God delivers not only directly but by empowering leaders and people, who will be supernaturally empowered by God to defend the city. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-12/

**v. 7**
- The Pulpit Commentary prefers the reading "as in former days" instead of "first," following the Greek, Latin and Syriac versions. If "first" is correct, the countryside is saved first so Jerusalem can't boast. Either way, each part shall have its share in the glory and honour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm
- Bible Hub's chapter study says God levels differences in status before he lifts up the royal house. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/zechariah/12.htm

**v. 8**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the weakest (literally "the one who stumbles") becomes a hero like David. The Greek Old Testament softens "like God" to "like the house of God." It applies the verse to the gifts given to every faithful member of Christ's church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm
- Matthew Henry: divine grace... makes weak saints to be not only good soldiers, but great soldiers, like David. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zec/Zec_012.cfm

**v. 9**
- The Pulpit Commentary takes "seek to destroy" as God's constant aim. It says the words could not have been written... while the dynasty of David reigned (that is on v. 7). On v. 9 it says no such alliance of nations ever attacked the literal Jerusalem, so it reads the verse about the church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm
- Precept Austin uses the same fact for the opposite conclusion: all nations have never yet come against Jerusalem, so this is still future. It quotes Cole that "seek" doesn't imply any doubt about the outcome. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah-12-commentary

**v. 10**

Traditional reading:
- **"Pour."** The Pulpit Commentary says the word suggests abundance (Joel 2:28). The house of David and Jerusalem stand for leaders and people alike. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm
- **Look first, then mourn.** Guzik draws this order from the verse and quotes Spurgeon: eyes are made for two things at least; first, to look with, and next, to weep with. The eye which looks to the pierced One is the eye which weeps for him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-12/
- **"Me" is the LORD.** Guzik notes the speaker is Yahweh, and adds that the Father sends the Spirit so that men will look upon the Son. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-12/
- **"Me" and "him."** The Pulpit Commentary says the switch from "Me" to "him" shows Jehovah speaking of the Messiah as a distinct Person. It sees the Messiah's two natures, God and man, in "Me whom they pierced." John 19:37 cites the verse at the crucifixion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm
- **Only son, firstborn.** The Pulpit Commentary says losing an only son was the heaviest blow a Hebrew family could suffer. "Firstborn" may echo the Passover and the death of Egypt's firstborn. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm
- **Who pierced him.** Gill says the piercing was done by the Jews' ancestors, or at their urging, and that converted Jews will one day look to him by faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/12-10.html
- **All sinners.** Matthew Henry applies the verse to every sinner, since our sins caused Christ's death. The genuine sorrows of a penitent soul flow from the believing sight of a pierced Saviour. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zec/Zec_012.cfm
- **The pierced one is the Lord.** Ligonier: This pierced one is none other than the Lord Himself, particularly the incarnate Son of God, as John teaches. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/mourning-over-pierced-lord

Where traditions differ:
- **When is it fulfilled?** This is the main split.
  - Future national conversion of Israel. Guzik links it to Romans 11:26 and says the Jewish people as a whole will welcome Jesus before he returns. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-12/ GotQuestions agrees: These events will occur at the end of the tribulation period at Christ's second coming. https://www.gotquestions.org/Zechariah-12-10-Messianic.html
  - Already begun. Coffman: Pentecost marked the amazing fulfillment of (1), meaning the outpouring of the Spirit. Benson (a Methodist commentator) says it has been fulfilled in some degree at least in the many ordinary Jews converted in the apostles' time. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/12-10.html
  - Ongoing through the church age. The Pulpit Commentary says the "looking" began at the cross, continued through the apostles' preaching, will go on until all Israel is converted, and is re-enacted whenever penitent sinners turn to Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm
  - Precept Austin (dispensational) attacks the Pulpit Commentary's and Leupold's "church" readings as replacement theology. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah-12-commentary
- **What is the "spirit of grace"?** Calvin (StudyLight labels Trapp's commentary "Calvinist"; Calvin himself is the classic Reformed voice) reads it first as God pouring out his own mercy. He then says the promise includes an internal light of faith, the author of which is the Spirit. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom30.iii.xiii.xiii.html Jamieson-Fausset-Brown instead says it is the Holy Spirit himself producing grace and prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Zec/Zec_012.cfm
- **Literal or spiritual?** Ligonier (Reformed) says that because John 19:37 shows a visible fulfilment, the rest of chapter 12 should be read as visible, historical events too. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/mourning-over-pierced-lord

Other views:
- **Text and translation.**
  - The Greek Old Testament reads "because they mocked me." https://biblehub.com/zechariah/12-10.htm
  - Benson notes 40–50 Hebrew manuscripts read "unto him." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/12-10.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary calls "him" a later change made for controversial reasons. It mentions critics who think Isaiah, Urijah or Jeremiah was the slain man, and rejects them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm
  - The NET Bible translates "the kingship of David" and "look to me." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=Zec+12%3A10%2C11&mode=text
- **Jewish interpretation.** Gill reports rabbis applying the verse to "Messiah son of Joseph," who would be slain. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/zechariah/12-10.html Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the Hebrew word always means literal piercing, against "rationalists" who follow the Greek "insulted." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Zec/Zec_012.cfm
- **"Look unto," not "upon."** Precept Austin quotes a teacher (not named in what I read) who says Israel will look *to* Christ by faith, not see him physically, and that Only then will He return. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah-12-commentary

**v. 11**
- **Josiah.** The usual reading is the national mourning for King Josiah, killed at Megiddo (2 Chronicles 35:20–25). The Pulpit Commentary calls the pagan-god explanation "preposterous." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/12.htm Barnes: in Josiah's death the last gleam of the sunset of Judah faded into night. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/12-11.html
- **Two mournings.** Gill reports the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) combining mourning for Ahab and for Josiah. He also gives Lightfoot's view that it recalls two great national laments. Constable says scholars have had trouble identifying the event. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/12-11.html
- **Modern scholarship.** Hastings' Dictionary takes it as mourning *for* a god, possibly Tammuz (Ezekiel 8:14). It also notes that Josiah was mourned in Jerusalem, not at Megiddo. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hdb/h/hadadrimmon.html The ISBE entry on NET Bible's site raises the same doubt. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=Hadad-Rimmon
- **Day of Atonement and Armageddon.** Guzik calls this the ultimate fulfilment of the Day of Atonement. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-12/ The Bible Says suggests the mention of Megiddo may hint that Israel's mourning will go hand in hand with Jesus' return. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/zec-12-v10-14.cfm

**vv. 12–14**
- Guzik: the mourning will be both very personal (each family on its own) and national. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-12/
- The Bible Says: listing particular clans shows how far and wide the sorrow reaches, and that Judah's rulers will recognise Jesus. It links this to "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:26). https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/zec-12-v10-14.cfm
- I didn't find commentary on who Nathan, Levi and Shimei were, or why wives mourn separately.
